summary: Redefines the format of message bodies to let multi-part, textual and non-textual content be represented and exchanged without loss of information. This was the original MIME specification, and it was replaced by RFC 1521.

eli5.summary: Email used to carry only plain text. MIME packs pictures, sounds and extra text into one message, with labels that tell the receiver what each piece is.

questions: what are the mime content types
subtitle: How email learned to carry pictures, sounds, attachments and non-ASCII text without breaking old mail systems.

tldr.problem: RFC 822 mail leaves the message body as flat, short-line, seven-bit ASCII text, so pictures, audio, attachments and most non-English text have no standard way to travel by email.
tldr.mechanism: MIME adds header fields (MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding) that label what a body is and how it was encoded for transport, plus a multipart type that packs several labelled parts into one message.
tldr.outcome: This is the original MIME specification, a Proposed Standard from June 1992. It was replaced by RFC 1521.

today: RFC 1341 is the original MIME specification, a Proposed Standard from June 1992, and it was obsoleted by RFC 1521. Read the newer document for the current definition.

sections.title: Why Mail Needed Extending
sections.content:
Since 1982, RFC 822 has defined the format of Internet text messages. It says nothing about non-text messages such as audio or images, and it is inadequate for languages that need character sets richer than US ASCII. Mail systems built on RFC 821 and RFC 822 also limit message contents to relatively short lines of seven-bit ASCII.

Users had to convert other data to printable ASCII themselves, using ad hoc encodings such as hexadecimal, uuencode or the base 64 scheme from RFC 1113. Gateways to X.400 mail had it worse: non-textual body parts were either converted to ASCII or discarded, so information was lost.

This document, by Borenstein and Freed, redefines the format of message bodies so that multi-part textual and non-textual bodies can be exchanged without loss of information. It stays compatible with RFC 822 mail. It does not extend mail header fields beyond US-ASCII; that is left to a companion document, RFC 1342.
sections.eli5: Old email was like a postcard that only fits a few lines of plain writing. MIME is the set of rules for putting photos, songs and other languages into the envelope too.

sections.title: MIME-Version and Content-Type Headers
sections.content:
A message written to this specification MUST carry the header MIME-Version: 1.0. It is required at the top level of a message, but not for each body part of a multipart entity.

The Content-Type header says what the body is, as type/subtype plus optional parameters, for example text/plain; charset=us-ascii. The type gives the general kind of data and the subtype the specific format, so a reader that does not know image/xyz still knows it is an image. A subtype is mandatory, and there are no default subtypes. Type, subtype and parameter names are not case sensitive.

Seven top-level types are defined: text, multipart, message, image, audio, video and application. Names starting with X- are private, and new standard subtypes are registered with IANA. When no Content-Type is given, a message is treated as text/plain; charset=us-ascii. A reader that meets an unknown type should treat it as application/octet-stream.

For text, the charset parameter names the character set. Its values are not case sensitive, and the default is US-ASCII.
sections.eli5: Every piece of mail gets a sticker saying what is inside, like 'photo' or 'plain words', so the receiving program knows how to show it.

sections.title: Content-Transfer-Encoding
sections.content:
Many useful types are naturally 8-bit or binary data, but RFC 821 restricts mail to 7-bit US-ASCII with 1000 character lines. The Content-Transfer-Encoding header says what reversible transformation was applied to make the body safe to transport. Its values are BASE64, QUOTED-PRINTABLE, 8BIT, 7BIT, BINARY or an X- token, and they are not case sensitive. 7BIT is assumed when the header is absent. The last three imply that no encoding was done; they only label the kind of data.

Quoted-Printable is the readable encoding, for data that is mostly printable ASCII. A byte can be written as = plus two uppercase hexadecimal digits (=3D for an equal sign). Encoded lines are at most 76 characters, and an = at the end of a line is a soft line break.

Base64 is the dense encoding for arbitrary bytes. Every 3 input bytes (24 bits) become 4 characters drawn from a 64-character alphabet, with = as padding at the end. The result is only about 33 percent larger than the input, and lines are at most 76 characters.

Creating new transfer encodings is explicitly and strongly discouraged. Multipart and message entities may only use a bit width or binary as their own encoding.
sections.eli5: Mail pipes only like simple letters. Base64 turns anything into simple letters, a bit like writing a picture out as a long code, and the other side turns it back.

sections.title: Multipart Messages
sections.content:
The multipart type puts several body parts in one message. Its one required parameter is boundary, 1 to 70 characters long. The encapsulation boundary is a line made of two hyphens followed by the boundary value, and it MUST NOT appear inside any part. The last part is followed by the same line with two more hyphens added. Text before the first boundary (the preamble) and after the last (the epilogue) is ignored.

Each body part looks like a small message: optional headers, a blank line, then the body. Only headers beginning with Content- have defined meaning there. A part with no headers is plain US-ASCII text.

Four subtypes are defined. mixed is for independent parts shown in order, and unrecognized subtypes are treated as mixed. alternative holds the same information in several formats, ordered with the preferred one last, and a reader should show the last one it can display. digest changes the default part type to message/rfc822. parallel asks for parts to be shown at the same time where possible.

The message type wraps a whole message and has the subtypes rfc822, partial (to split a large body across messages) and External-body (to point at data held elsewhere).
sections.eli5: Multipart is a box with dividers. Each compartment holds one thing, and a special divider line shows where one thing ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Minimal MIME Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC does not expect every implementation to support every type. Appendix A instead defines a minimum for a MIME-conformant mail user agent. It MUST always generate MIME-Version: 1.0, recognize and decode quoted-printable and base64, encode non-seven-bit data with one of them, interpret Content-Type and avoid showing users raw data of types other than text, and be able to send at least text/plain with the character set given as a parameter if it is not US-ASCII.

It must also handle the predefined types to stated minimum extents, for example recognizing the ISO-8859-* character sets well enough to display characters shared with US-ASCII.
sections.eli5: Nobody has to understand every kind of attachment. There is just a short list of things every mail program must at least manage, so mail between different programs still works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section is short. It points to Section 7.4.2 and Appendix G and asks implementors to pay special attention to any content type that can cause remote execution of actions in the recipient's environment.

The model case is application/postscript. The RFC says that running general-purpose PostScript interpreters entails serious security risks, and that implementors are discouraged from simply sending PostScript email bodies to off-the-shelf interpreters. Sending PostScript to a printer is usually safe because the potential for harm is greatly constrained.
sections.eli5: Some attachments are really little programs. Opening one without care is like letting a stranger press buttons on your computer, so mail programs should be careful with those.

viz.caption: THE FIVE STANDARD TRANSFER ENCODING VALUES

cells: Already short lines of US-ASCII; the default, no encoding done
Short lines, but non-ASCII octets may appear; no encoding done
Non-ASCII and lines of any length; no encoding done
Dense encoding for arbitrary octets, about 33 percent larger

data.title: Same message in three formats
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary=boundary42

--boundary42
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii

...plain text version of message goes here....

--boundary42
Content-Type: text/richtext

.... richtext version of same message goes here ...
--boundary42
Content-Type: text/x-whatever

.... fanciest formatted version of same  message  goes  here
...
--boundary42--
